metadata.title: The Relationship Between Weekly Instruction, Homework Time and Students’ Competences

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 fourth-grade data from 58 countries and applies TIMSS recommended practices to account for the two-stage cluster sampling design. In the estimation, the authors state that they use student sampling weights and jackknife replication weights to correct standard errors. The analytic sample is restricted to students with non-missing teacher-reported weekly instruction and weekly homework time (with a robustness check showing no strong selection bias in socio-economic characteristics between missing and non-missing teacher-information groups). Because the models are student fixed-effects regressions rather than ML algorithms, the paper does not discuss any ML-specific weighting limitations; instead it follows TIMSS guidance for weighted inference.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are constructed standardized cognitive scores based on students’ actual responses (not TIMSS imputed plausible values), and the paper does not describe a missing-data imputation strategy for item nonresponse or other missing covariates. While the authors discuss excluding students with missing teacher information on weekly instruction/homework time, they do not provide a full missing-data handling protocol for all variables used in the fixed-effects models. This is therefore a reporting gap for missingness beyond the teacher-time variables.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses TIMSS 2019 fourth-grade mathematics and science data for 58 participating countries. It restricts to students with teacher-reported weekly minutes of instruction time and weekly minutes of assigned homework time (converted to weekly hours) for both subjects, because these are required for the within-student between-subjects fixed-effects differencing. The authors also note that students whose teachers do not provide information on weekly instruction or homework time are excluded; they report a selection-bias check using socio-economic characteristics between included and missing-teacher-information groups. To avoid bias from TIMSS imputed item scores, the authors construct alternative standardized cognitive scores using only students’ actual responses (correct/partially correct/incorrect) and standardize scores using each country’s mean and standard deviation for each subject.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Mathematics & Science (student fixed-effects; standardized cognitive scores)
main_findings.target_variable: Instruction time effect on competence (standardized cognitive scores)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Country-specific fixed-effects coefficients (SD units per +1 weekly hour) reported in Table 1: range from -0.088 (Armenia) to 0.126 (Poland); most countries non-significant (44/58).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Mathematics & Science the study leveraged weekly instruction time (with within-student between-subjects fixed-effects and controls including student confidence/liking indices) to estimate the effect on standardized cognitive competence scores, finding that one additional hour of weekly instruction time is non-significant in most countries and only low positive effects appear in some (e.g., Canada, Czech Republic, Spain, Turkey, USA). This indicates that simply increasing weekly instruction time may not reliably improve primary competences, and that competence-oriented curriculum and instructional quality may be more important than time quantity.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Mathematics & Science (student fixed-effects; standardized cognitive scores)
main_findings.target_variable: Homework time effect on competence (standardized cognitive scores)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Country-specific fixed-effects coefficients (SD units per +1 weekly hour) reported in Table 1: range from -0.037 (Qatar) to 0.166 (England); most countries non-significant (40/58).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Mathematics & Science the study leveraged weekly homework time (with within-student between-subjects fixed-effects and controls including student confidence/liking indices) to estimate the effect on standardized cognitive competence scores, finding that one additional hour of weekly homework time is non-significant in most countries and shows low positive effects in some (e.g., Australia, England, Germany, Hong Kong, Japan, Singapore, USA) with a low negative effect in Qatar. This indicates that increasing homework time is unlikely to improve primary competences broadly, and that homework policies should be competence-oriented and potentially reduced where additional time does not translate into gains.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes TIMSS 2019 fourth-grade mathematics and science data for 58 countries (N=276,512) to test whether one additional weekly hour of instruction time and homework time is associated with students’ competences. Using student fixed-effects within-students between-subjects differencing (and constructing standardized cognitive scores from students’ actual responses to avoid bias from TIMSS imputed scores), the authors estimate country-specific effects in SD units per +1 hour. Results in Table 1 show that instruction time is non-significant in most countries (44/58) with coefficients ranging from −0.088 (Armenia) to 0.126 (Poland), while homework time is non-significant in most countries (40/58) with coefficients ranging from −0.037 (Qatar) to 0.166 (England). The paper applies TIMSS recommended sampling weights and jackknife replication for standard errors, but it does not provide a comprehensive missing-data handling protocol beyond excluding students with missing teacher time information. The fixed-effects approach reduces confounding from time-invariant student factors, yet the authors caution against strong causal interpretation.
